title: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone
hookLine: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone

lines: SOMEONE ON THE CORNER AT SEVEN.
cards: Anyone who's tried to change a habit alone knows how it goes. Day one, fired up. Day four, a little tired.
Day nine, you skip once, then twice, and nobody notices, because nobody knew. Then there are the times something actually stuck. Very often, someone else was in it.
A running buddy who'd be standing on the corner at seven. A friend who'd ask, did you do it? A group that noticed when you weren't there.
Many of the world's traditions, for all their differences, say it in their own words: you can't do this alone.

teach.h: NOT HALF. THE WHOLE OF IT.
teach.b: There's a conversation in the early Buddhist texts that surprises people. The Buddha's attendant, Ananda, says that good friendship, having admirable companions, must be half of the spiritual life.
The Buddha corrects him. Not half, he says. It's the whole of it.

The Hebrew Bible says it plainly: "Two are better than one". And then the picture: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up."

teach.h: A MINYAN, A CONGREGATION, A SANGAT.
teach.b: In Jewish practice, some prayers, like the mourner's Kaddish, are traditionally said only with a minyan, a group of ten. You need other people just to say them.

In Islam, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught that prayer offered together in congregation is worth many times more than prayer offered alone; one well-known report puts it at twenty-seven times.
Sikhs speak of the sangat, the gathered community, and Christians of the church, meaning the gathered people, not only the building.

And a long-running study at Harvard has followed hundreds of people for more than eighty years. When its directors are asked what best predicts who stays healthy and happy into old age, their answer isn't money or fame.
It's the quality of people's relationships. So a sit on your own with an app is a real start. But each of these homes adds something: find your people.

how: Many traditions practice together: Buddhists speak of the sangha and good friendship, Jews gather a minyan for key prayers, Muslims pray in congregation, Sikhs gather as the sangat, and Christians meet as a church.

games.q: you can't do this alone — tap the pairs.

games.q: you're Ananda, and you tell the Buddha that good friendship must be half of the spiritual life. what does he say?
o: no, it's only a small part.
not half. it's the whole of it.
games.why: not half: the whole of the spiritual life, he says, is having admirable friends and companions.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For about seventy-five seconds, bring to mind the people who've lifted you up when you fell.
One at a time. A face, a name, a moment. Then let one more face come: someone you'd like to walk this path with, even a little.
Don't plan anything. Just let them arrive. If you pray, you can hold them there.

wordCard.voice: Company. The people who lift you up when you fall, and the ones who notice when you're not there. Twentieth word.

orig.note: Pali, from the Buddhist tradition, kalyāṇa-mittatā: admirable friendship, having good companions on the path.

carryVoice: Your line: find your people. Someone who notices when you're not there is worth a lot. Tomorrow, camp one closes.
